On-Chain Operator. Lesson 3.1: How lending markets work. The frame is navy and cyan. You will see one idea at a time, then write it down. Education only.

Here's the plan. What a money market actually is, mechanically, and where the yield genuinely comes from. Utilisation, and the kinked interest-rate curve it drives. A full worked example, with a real, verified rate table. And why a sudden spike in rates near full utilisation is a warning sign, not a gift.
The mechanism.

Here's the mechanism, in full. Lenders supply assets into a shared pool. Borrowers borrow from that same pool, against collateral they've locked up. A smart contract sets the rates on both sides, automatically. And when you supply, you receive a receipt token back, representing your deposit plus the interest it's earning, growing in value the whole time you hold it.

Here's exactly where the yield genuinely comes from, since it isn't magic, and it isn't the protocol's own money. Every dollar a lender earns is a dollar a borrower actually paid, in interest, for the privilege of borrowing against their own collateral instead of selling it. No borrower, no yield. It's a direct transfer, mediated by a smart contract, not manufactured out of nowhere.

Here's exactly what happens to your receipt token, step by step, from the moment you supply. You deposit an asset, and receive a receipt token in return, immediately. That token's exchange rate against the underlying asset climbs continuously, as interest accrues, second by second. You never need to claim interest separately, or take any additional action.
And when you eventually redeem it, you receive back more of the underlying asset than you originally put in.

Worth contrasting this against a traditional bank loan, since it explains why DeFi lending works so differently underneath. A bank lends based on your credit history and income, trusting you to repay over time, with no collateral locked up front. A DeFi money market instead requires collateral worth more than the loan, upfront, and enforces repayment through code, not trust or credit checks.

Quick check. Where does a lender's yield in a money market actually come from? The answer: directly from the interest borrowers pay to borrow against their collateral. It's a transfer between the two sides, not money created by the protocol.
The kinked interest-rate curve.

Here's exactly what utilisation is, and what it does, mechanically. Utilisation equals the amount currently borrowed, divided by the total amount supplied. Below a market's chosen optimal point, commonly around eighty percent, rates rise only gently as utilisation climbs. Above that same optimal point, the curve kinks, and rates rise steeply instead, specifically to pull in more lenders and push out some borrowers.

Worth naming the trade-off from each side's perspective directly, since “gentle then steep” affects lenders and borrowers differently. A lender below the optimal point earns a modest, steady rate; above it, a much richer one, but with growing liquidity risk attached. A borrower below the optimal point pays a modest, predictable rate; above it, a rate that can climb sharply, fast enough to force an unplanned repayment.

Worth being precise about why the curve is deliberately shaped this way, rather than a straight line the whole way. A smooth, straight-line curve gives the market no urgent signal as it approaches full utilisation, the exact moment lenders might not be able to withdraw at all. The kink is a deliberate design choice: make the pain sharp and sudden, specifically where the actual danger, illiquidity, begins.

One more piece worth naming before the worked example: supply A.P.Y. is never quite the same as borrow A.P.Y., even at the same utilisation. Supply A.P.Y. is roughly borrow A.P.Y., times utilisation, times one minus the reserve factor, the protocol's own cut. That reserve factor is exactly why lenders always earn somewhat less than what borrowers are actually paying.

Here's how to actually check a market's own kink point yourself, since it isn't the same on every protocol or every asset. Open the market's own interface or documentation directly. Look specifically for its “optimal utilisation” or “kink” parameter, usually shown as a percentage. And compare that number against the market's current utilisation, so you know how much room actually remains before rates start climbing steeply.

Quick check. Why does the interest-rate curve kink sharply above the optimal utilisation point, instead of rising smoothly the whole way? The answer: to make borrowing expensive and supplying attractive right when liquidity runs low, restoring withdrawal capacity before the market actually locks up.
Worked example.

Here's the actual curve, plotted from this specific illustrative example: four percent borrow A.P.Y. at eighty percent optimal utilisation, then a sixty-percent slope above it. At fifty percent utilisation, borrow A.P.Y. is two point five percent. At seventy percent, three point five percent. At eighty percent, exactly four percent, the kink itself.
And then it launches: ninety percent utilisation reaches thirty-four percent borrow A.P.Y., and ninety-five percent reaches forty-nine percent.

Now put supply A.P.Y. next to that same borrow A.P.Y., at a ten-percent reserve factor, since lenders never see the full number. At eighty percent utilisation: four percent borrow, two point nine percent supply. At ninety-five percent: forty-nine percent borrow, but supply climbs just as dramatically, to roughly forty-two percent, since supply A.P.Y. scales directly with that same borrow rate.

One real, dated event, so this isn't a hypothetical risk. Major lending markets have genuinely experienced episodes of utilisation pushing well above ninety percent during periods of high demand, with supply rates spiking sharply and withdrawal delays reported by users. This is outside research, not this program's own data, but it's exactly the scenario this worked example is built to help you recognise before it happens to you.

And here's the actual warning hidden inside that second number. A sudden forty-two-percent supply A.P.Y. looks like an incredible yield, right up until you remember what it actually means: the pool is nearly fully borrowed, and lenders may simply not be able to withdraw, because the money is out, lent to borrowers who haven't repaid yet. A sudden high supply APY is often a warning, not a gift.

Here's exactly what unfolds, step by step, as utilisation actually climbs toward one hundred percent, so “lenders may not be able to withdraw” isn't just a phrase. Utilisation climbs past the optimal point. Rates spike steeply, exactly as the kink is designed to do. Some lenders, seeing high rates, try to withdraw, but the pool's available liquidity is shrinking.
And once utilisation is high enough, some withdrawals simply queue, or fail outright, until borrowers repay or new supply arrives.

Quick check. Utilisation on a lending market is ninety-nine percent. What's the actual risk for lenders right now? The answer: withdrawals may be blocked entirely, until borrowers repay or new supply arrives, since almost all of the pool's assets are currently lent out.

Here's your checklist. Do it now, before supplying to any market. Check the market's current utilisation before you supply, not after. Know that specific market's optimal-utilisation kink, since it isn't the same everywhere. And treat any sudden rate spike as a liquidity warning to investigate, never as a gift to celebrate.

One last honest connection, before the recap, since this lesson sits right underneath everything else in Module Three. Every borrow you'll model in the lessons ahead, health factor, leveraged loops, perpetual futures, ultimately draws on the exact same pool mechanism and the exact same curve this lesson just walked through. Understanding this curve well is what makes the rest of the module make sense, not a detail to skip past.

Let's recap. A money market is a pool: lenders supply, borrowers borrow against collateral, a contract sets both rates. Every dollar of yield a lender earns is a dollar a borrower actually paid; it's a transfer, not created money. The interest-rate curve kinks deliberately above an optimal utilisation point, to protect withdrawal capacity right when it matters most.
And a sudden spike in supply APY, near full utilisation, is a liquidity warning first, an opportunity second, if at all.
Check utilisation before you supply, and treat any sudden rate spike as a warning worth investigating first. Next up, Lesson three point two: LTV, liquidation threshold and health factor.

beats.vo: Lesson three point two. L.T.V., liquidation threshold, and health factor. These three numbers decide whether a loan is a tool, or a trap.

Education only, not financial advice. Crypto and DeFi carry significant risk, including total loss of capital. This is general information. On-Chain Operator. Lesson 3.2: LTV, liquidation threshold & health factor. The frame is navy and cyan. You will see one idea at a time, then write it down. Education only.

Here's the uncomfortable truth about borrowing on-chain. A lending protocol never calls you. There's no margin call, no grace period, and no one to negotiate with. When your collateral falls too far, it's sold automatically, at a penalty. So the only protection you have is arithmetic you did before you borrowed.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to do three things. Measure your loan-to-value and health factor for any position. Locate the exact price at which you'd be liquidated. And defend the position, by choosing a buffer and a plan before you borrow a single dollar.

Every lending position comes down to four numbers. First, L.T.V., or loan-to-value. It's simply your debt divided by the value of your collateral. Second, max L.T.V. That's the most the protocol lets you borrow against an asset. Third, the liquidation threshold. That's the loan-to-value at which your position can be liquidated, and it's always set higher than max L.T.V. Fourth, the health factor.
Collateral value, times the liquidation threshold, divided by your debt.

If you remember one thing, remember this. When the health factor falls below one, your position is liquidatable. Above one, you're safe, for now. At one or below, anyone can repay part of your debt, and take some of your collateral at a discount. That discount is the penalty, and you pay it.

People mix up the two limits, so let's separate them. Max L.T.V. is a borrowing limit. It stops you taking on more debt, and on its own it can't hurt you. The liquidation threshold is a trigger. Cross it, and liquidation starts. That's where you actually lose collateral.

Let's work a real example, step by step. You deposit ten E.T.H. at three thousand dollars each. Your collateral is worth thirty thousand dollars. You borrow twelve thousand dollars of stablecoins. Loan-to-value is twelve thousand, divided by thirty thousand. That's forty percent. The liquidation threshold is point eight, so the health factor is thirty thousand, times point eight, divided by twelve thousand. That's exactly two.

And the liquidation price is your debt, divided by your quantity times the threshold. Twelve thousand, divided by eight. That's fifteen hundred dollars. So E.T.H. can fall fifty percent before you're liquidated.

Now watch what happens as you borrow more. Aim for a health factor of one and a half, and your debt can be sixteen thousand dollars. Your liquidation price rises to two thousand. A thirty-three percent drop now liquidates you. Suppose, as an illustration, the market lets you borrow up to seventy-five percent. That's twenty-two thousand five hundred dollars.

The health factor is twenty-four thousand, divided by twenty-two thousand five hundred. About one point oh seven. Your liquidation price becomes two thousand, eight hundred and twelve dollars. A drop of just over six percent. Crypto can move that much in an hour. Borrowing the maximum leaves almost no room.

Here's the same story as a picture. The horizontal axis is the price of E.T.H. The vertical axis is your health factor. Start at today, three thousand dollars, where the blue line sits at a health factor of two. Follow the blue line down and left, and it crosses one at fifteen hundred dollars. That's your liquidation price. Now the orange line, with sixteen thousand of debt.
It starts lower, and it hits one at two thousand dollars. More debt doesn't just lower the line. It moves the cliff edge closer to where you're standing.

And here's why the buffer matters more than it looks. Liquidations sell collateral into a falling market. That selling pushes the price lower, which triggers the next set of liquidations. A cascade. The move that reaches your liquidation price is often faster and deeper than anyone expected. Your buffer is the time you have to react.

When the health factor falls, you have three ways to raise it. Repay debt. That's the most direct fix, so keep some stablecoins ready for it. Add collateral, from a reserve you set aside before you borrowed. Or the cheapest defence of all: borrow less in the first place. Decide which lever you'll pull, and at what health factor, before you open the position. Not during the crash.

Four mistakes cause most liquidations. Borrowing right up to max L.T.V., because the button allows it. Forgetting that interest keeps growing the debt, so the health factor drifts down even when prices don't move. Having no alert, or an alert that fires while you're asleep. And having no reserve, so when the moment comes there's nothing to repay or top up with.

Here's your checklist for this lesson. Health factor and liquidation price calculated before borrowing. A health factor of at least two for volatile collateral. And alerts set, which we build properly in Module fourteen, lesson one.

Question one. Collateral is worth fifty thousand dollars, the liquidation threshold is point eight, and the debt is twenty thousand. What's the health factor? The answer: two. Fifty thousand times point eight is forty thousand, divided by twenty thousand.
Question two. Why keep the health factor well above one? The answer: collateral prices can fall fast. The buffer is your time to react.
Question three. What's the difference between max L.T.V. and the liquidation threshold? The answer: max L.T.V. caps new borrowing. The liquidation threshold is where liquidation becomes possible.

Let's recap. A health factor below one means liquidatable. Your liquidation price is your debt, divided by quantity times the liquidation threshold. More debt moves the cliff closer, fast. And your buffer, and your plan, are decided before you borrow. Never during the crash.
Do the checklist now, with the calculator, before you move on. Next up, lesson three point three: liquidations and cascades, and how to survive them.

On-Chain Operator. Lesson 3.3: Liquidations and cascades. The frame is navy and cyan. You will see one idea at a time, then write it down. Education only.

Here's the plan. Exactly what a liquidator does, mechanically, the moment your health factor crosses below one. How a single liquidation can actually trigger a cascade of more. A full worked example, continuing directly from Lesson three point two's own position. And the written defence ladder that keeps you from ever needing to find out what any of this actually costs.
What a liquidator actually does.

Here's exactly what happens, the instant your health factor drops below one. A liquidator, almost always a bot watching for exactly this, repays part of your debt, up to a limit called the close factor, often fifty percent. In exchange, it seizes collateral worth that same repaid amount, plus a bonus, the liquidation penalty, often five to ten percent.
That bonus is the liquidator's profit, and it comes directly out of what would otherwise have been your collateral.

Here's that same sequence, broken into its four actual steps, since “liquidator” can sound abstract until you see the mechanics. Your health factor crosses below one. A bot notices, essentially instantly; this is automated, competitive, and fast. It repays up to the close factor of your debt.
And it seizes collateral worth that repayment, plus the bonus, leaving you with less collateral and less debt, but a real loss on the bonus itself.

One real number, so this isn't a rare edge case. Blockchain analytics have tracked billions of dollars in total liquidations across major lending protocols, cumulatively, since DeFi lending began. This is outside research, not this program's own data, but it's exactly why this lesson's defence ladder is worth writing down now, not after your first close call.

Quick check. What does a liquidator actually receive, in exchange for repaying part of your debt? The answer: collateral equal to the debt it repaid, plus a bonus, the liquidation penalty, often five to ten percent, which is a real loss to you.
Cascades.

Here's exactly how a cascade actually forms, step by step, since it's the mechanism that turns an isolated event into a market-wide one. A liquidation sells seized collateral, immediately, into the open market. That sale itself pushes the price down further, the same price-impact mechanism from Module two. That further price drop pushes other, separate positions below their own health-factor line.
And those get liquidated too, selling more collateral, into an already-falling price.

Worth being precise about why this matters even if your own position feels perfectly safe. A cascade isn't really about any single borrower's mistake; it's a mechanical feedback loop, forced selling causing more forced selling, that can move a market meaningfully in a short window. It's exactly why a comfortable buffer matters most during genuinely volatile periods, not just on an average day.

Worth naming, plainly, that cascades aren't a theoretical risk this lesson invented. DeFi lending markets have genuinely experienced sharp, fast periods of concentrated liquidations during major market drops, with total liquidation volume spiking well above a typical day's level in a matter of hours. This is outside research, illustrative of the pattern, not a specific claim about any one event, but the pattern itself is well documented.

Quick check. What's the actual mechanism that turns one liquidation into a cascade of more? The answer: liquidations sell collateral into the market, pushing the price down, which pushes other, separate positions below their own health-factor line, triggering further liquidations.
Worked example.

Here's the exact position this worked example continues from Lesson three point two. Ten E.T.H., thirty thousand dollars of collateral, twelve thousand dollars of debt, a health factor of two. Now E.T.H. falls to one thousand four hundred ninety dollars, just under the fifteen-hundred-dollar liquidation price. Health factor is now just under one.

Now watch exactly what the liquidator does, in this specific case, step by step. It repays six thousand dollars, fifty percent of your twelve-thousand-dollar debt, the close factor. It seizes collateral worth six thousand dollars, times one point zero five, the five-percent bonus, which is six thousand three hundred dollars.
At one thousand four hundred ninety dollars per E.T.H., that's roughly four point two two eight E.T.H., seized from your position.

Worth being precise about what that three hundred dollars actually represents, since it's easy to gloss past as a small number. It's not a fee for a service you needed. It's value that leaves your position specifically because you didn't act first, on top of having your collateral sold, involuntarily, near the low of that exact price move. The bonus is the entire reason self-deleveraging beats being liquidated.

Worth naming what's actually left of your position after this specific liquidation, since fifty percent repaid isn't the whole story. Your debt drops from twelve thousand to six thousand dollars. Your collateral drops by that roughly four point two two eight E.T.H. seized. If price keeps falling from here, health factor can cross below one again, and the exact same process can repeat, on what's left.

Quick check. Why is choosing to sell some of your own collateral yourself, before liquidation, better than letting it happen automatically? The answer: you avoid the liquidation penalty entirely, and you choose the size and timing yourself, instead of a bot forcing both on you.
The defence ladder.

Here's the actual ladder, with exact health-factor levels, written down before you ever need it, not decided under pressure. At health factor two point zero: an alert fires, nothing else yet. At one point seven: repay from a reserve you've already set aside, or add more collateral. At one point five: sell part of your collateral yourself, deliberately, on your own terms.
And never, under any circumstance, wait until one point one to start acting.

Here's what actually setting up that health-factor-two alert looks like, in practice, from the ladder's very first rung. Open your protocol's own notification settings, or a third-party monitoring tool, covered fully in Module fourteen point one. Set a trigger at your own chosen health-factor level. Point it at a channel you'll actually see quickly, not one you check once a week.
And test it once, deliberately, so you know it actually works before you need it to.

Worth being precise about what “repay from reserve” at HF 1.7 actually buys you, versus waiting. Repaying debt directly raises health factor immediately, by the same formula from Lesson three point two, without touching your collateral at all. Adding collateral instead raises it too, but ties up more capital. Either move, taken at 1.7, costs nothing beyond the capital itself.
The same move, forced at 1.1, costs the liquidation penalty on top.

Put the two paths side by side, at the exact same starting point, since the entire lesson comes down to this choice. Wait, and a bot decides the size, the timing, and takes a bonus on top, at whatever price the market happens to be at that moment.
Act at one point five, and you choose the size, the timing, and keep the full value of what you sell, no penalty attached.

Here's your checklist. Do it now, before you ever need it. Your defence ladder is written, with exact health-factor levels, not vague intentions. A reserve is actually set aside to repay from, covered fully in Module twelve point four. And you know your collateral's specific price oracle, covered in Module five point three, since that's what actually decides when liquidation triggers.

One last honest connection before the recap, since this ladder is only as good as the reserve behind it. Rung two of the ladder, repay from reserve, assumes that reserve genuinely exists, already funded, before health factor ever gets there. A defence ladder with an empty reserve rung is really just a two-step ladder, with a gap exactly where you need it most.

Let's recap. A liquidator repays part of your debt, up to the close factor, and seizes that value in collateral, plus a bonus, a real loss to you. Cascades form because liquidations sell into the market, pushing prices down, triggering more liquidations. In the worked example, a fall to fourteen ninety cost three hundred dollars in bonus alone, on top of an involuntary sale near the low.
And the defence ladder, written with exact HF levels, is what keeps you from ever finding any of that out the hard way.
Write your defence ladder now, with exact health-factor levels, before you ever need it under pressure. Next up, Lesson three point four: Borrowing strategies and looping.

On-Chain Operator. Lesson 3.4: Borrowing strategies & looping. The frame is navy and cyan. You will see one idea at a time, then write it down. Education only.

Here's the plan. Borrowing for liquidity, without ever selling what you hold. Looping, mechanically, and the leverage formula it actually produces. Correlated loops versus volatile ones, and why that distinction matters more than the leverage number itself. And a full worked example, with real numbers, showing exactly when a loop's return gets wiped out.
Liquidity without selling.

Here's the actual use case borrowing solves, worth naming plainly before looping at all. You hold an asset you want to keep, long-term, but you need cash now, for something else entirely. Instead of selling, and losing your position, and potentially triggering a taxable event, you borrow stablecoins against it, keep the asset locked as collateral, and repay later.
Module twelve point three turns this exact habit into a real, written credit policy.

Put a real example side by side with the alternative, to make “liquidity without selling” concrete. Sell ten thousand dollars of an asset for cash, and you've lost that entire position, permanently, plus potentially triggered a taxable event on any gain.
Borrow five thousand dollars against that same ten thousand instead, and you keep the full position, still growing if the asset does, while the cash need is met either way.

Quick check. What's the core benefit of borrowing stablecoins against an asset, instead of selling it? The answer: you get liquidity now, without losing your position in the asset, and without triggering a sale you didn't actually want to make.
Looping.

Here's exactly what a loop does, mechanically, one full cycle at a time. Deposit an asset as collateral. Borrow against it, up to some chosen L.T.V. Use what you borrowed to buy more of the same asset. And re-deposit that, as more collateral, starting the exact same cycle again, one loop deeper each time.

Here's the formula that falls directly out of repeating that cycle, worth seeing in full before the worked example. After n loops at L.T.V. L, your leverage equals one minus L to the power of n plus one, all divided by one minus L. More loops push you closer and closer to a ceiling; at L.T.V.
zero point seven five, that ceiling is exactly four times leverage, no matter how many additional loops you run.

Plot leverage against the number of loops, at an L.T.V. of zero point seven specifically, and you can watch that ceiling actually being approached. One loop: one point seven times. Three loops: two point five three times, exactly this lesson's worked example. Five loops: two point nine four times.
And ten loops: three point two seven times, closing in on, but never quite reaching, the three point three three times ceiling.

Quick check. What's the maximum possible leverage from looping at an LTV of 0.75, however many loops you run? The answer: four times, exactly one divided by one minus zero point seven five, the ceiling the formula approaches as loops increase, but never exceeds.
Correlated vs volatile loops.

Here's the actual distinction that decides how dangerous any given loop really is, more than the leverage number alone ever does. A correlated loop, an L.S.T. against its own underlying asset, or one stablecoin against another, moves both sides together, almost in lockstep. A volatile-against-stable loop instead has collateral and debt that can move in completely opposite directions, which is exactly what actually threatens your health factor.

Worth naming concrete examples of each, so “correlated” isn't just an abstract label. A liquid-staking token looped against its own underlying, an L.S.T. of E.T.H. against E.T.H. itself, is a correlated loop; both sides track the same underlying price, closely. E.T.H. looped against U.S.D.C. debt is a volatile-against-stable loop; E.T.H.'s price can move sharply while the U.S.D.C. debt stays exactly flat.

Here's exactly why that correlation matters so directly to your safety, mechanically, not just intuitively. Health factor depends on your collateral's value relative to your debt. If both move together, in the same direction, by roughly the same amount, that ratio barely changes, even at high leverage. If they diverge instead, the exact same leverage multiple becomes dramatically more dangerous, far faster.
Worked example.

Here's the one relationship this entire lesson comes down to, visually. A leveraged loop's return depends entirely on the spread between what your collateral earns, and what your borrowed debt costs. Widen that spread, and leverage amplifies a genuinely good return. Narrow it, or let it flip negative, and the exact same leverage amplifies a loss just as fast.

Here's the setup this entire worked example runs on. L.T.V. zero point seven, three loops, three point five percent collateral yield, two point five percent borrow rate. Run through this program's own calculator, and leverage comes out to two point five three times.

Now the net A.P.Y. on equity, step by step, the formula that actually tells you whether this loop was worth doing. Collateral yield, times leverage: three point five percent, times two point five three, is eight point eight six percent. Borrow rate, times leverage minus one: two point five percent, times one point five three, is three point eight three percent. Subtract the second from the first, and net A.P.Y.
on equity is five point zero three percent.

Now find the exact point where that positive return actually disappears, since rates don't stay fixed forever. At a two point five percent borrow rate, net A.P.Y. on equity is five point zero three percent, genuinely positive. Raise the borrow rate to five point seven eight percent, with nothing else changed, and that same loop's net return on equity hits exactly zero.

And here's exactly why that break-even number should worry you, not just interest you, given what Lesson three point one already showed. Borrow rates on a nearly-full pool can jump from around four percent to thirty-four percent, within hours, not months, exactly the kinked-curve mechanism from that same lesson.
A loop that looks comfortably profitable today can be underwater by tomorrow morning, with nothing about your own position having changed at all.

Quick check. What single number actually decides whether a loop is worth doing, more than the leverage multiple itself? The answer: the spread between collateral yield and borrow rate. A wide, stable spread makes a loop worthwhile; a narrow or shrinking one erases the return.

Here's how to actually monitor an open loop, ongoing, not just at the moment you set it up. Check the current spread, collateral yield minus borrow rate, on a regular schedule, not only when something feels wrong. Watch for utilisation climbing on the borrow side specifically, since that's the exact signal from Lesson three point one that rates are about to move.
And unwind, deliberately, the moment the spread turns negative, rather than waiting to see if it recovers.

Here's your checklist. Do it now, before opening any loop. Name your actual repayment source, before you ever borrow, not as an afterthought. Only loop correlated pairs, and stay below the mathematical maximum leverage for your L.T.V. And know your specific break-even borrow rate, with an alert actually set on it, not just calculated once and forgotten.

One last honest connection before the recap, tying looping directly back to Lesson three point two. Every loop still carries a health factor, exactly like any other borrow, and the exact same liquidation mechanics from Lesson three point three still apply, on the full, leveraged position, not just the original deposit. Looping doesn't create a new category of risk. It multiplies the familiar one.

Let's recap. Borrowing against an asset gets you liquidity without selling it, a deliberate credit policy, not a reaction. Looping multiplies exposure through repeated deposit-borrow cycles, approaching a leverage ceiling that never exceeds one over one minus L.T.V. Correlated pairs keep health factor stable even at high leverage; volatile-against-stable pairs don't.
And the spread between collateral yield and borrow rate, not the leverage number alone, decides whether any given loop was actually worth doing.
Name your repayment source, loop only correlated pairs, and know your break-even borrow rate before you open anything. Next up, Lesson three point five: Perpetual futures and margin on-chain.

beats.vo: Lesson three point five. Perpetual futures and margin on-chain. By the end, you'll understand perp positions well enough to use them for hedging and carry, and to see exactly why high leverage fails.

Education only, not financial advice. Crypto and DeFi carry significant risk, including total loss of capital. This is general information. It does not consider your objectives, financial situation, or needs. Past or example results do not indicate future results. Consider independent advice. We do not sell or run a trading bot. Leverage magnifies losses. A leveraged position can be liquidated, and you can lose all the money you commit.
On-Chain Operator. Lesson 3.5: Perpetual futures and margin on-chain. The frame is navy and cyan. You will see one idea at a time, then write it down. Education only.

Here's the plan. What a perpetual future actually is, and the two margin modes you can choose between. Mark price, index price, and funding, the three mechanics that keep a perp tracking spot with no expiry. The liquidation formula, and what it actually does at high leverage. And a full worked example, with real numbers, showing exactly how little room high leverage leaves you.
What a perp actually is.

Here's a perpetual future, in full. It tracks an asset's price, with no expiry date, unlike a traditional futures contract that settles on a fixed day. You post margin, collateral backing the position, and choose leverage, a multiplier on your exposure relative to that margin. Higher leverage means more exposure, and controls, per dollar posted, but leaves proportionally less room before liquidation.

Here's the actual choice you make, before opening any perp position, between the two margin modes. Isolated margin risks only the margin you specifically put into that one position; a bad trade there can't touch the rest of your account. Cross margin instead backs every open position with your entire account balance, meaning one badly wrong trade can genuinely drain everything else you're holding open.

Quick check. What's the actual difference between isolated and cross margin? The answer: isolated margin risks only that specific position's own margin. Cross margin puts your whole account behind every open position at once.
Mark, index, and funding.

Here's what these three actually do, and why each one matters differently. Index price is the reference, pulled from spot markets elsewhere, what the asset is genuinely worth right now. Mark price is a smoothed version used specifically for liquidation decisions, designed to resist brief, manipulated price spikes.
And funding is a periodic payment, usually every hour or every eight hours, between longs and shorts, that keeps the perp's price from drifting too far from index over time.

Worth being precise about why liquidation uses mark price specifically, not index price directly, since it's an easy detail to overlook. A brief, thin-liquidity spike on one venue could otherwise trigger liquidations that shouldn't happen at all. Mark price smooths that out. But it also means your liquidation can technically trigger at a slightly different number than the headline spot price you're watching elsewhere.

Quick check. Which price actually triggers your liquidation, mark or index? The answer: mark price, specifically because it's smoothed to resist brief, manipulated spikes that index price alone wouldn't filter out.
The liquidation formula.

Here's the formula, and exactly what it does to your room to be wrong as leverage climbs. Take one, divided by your leverage. Subtract your maintenance margin, the minimum buffer the exchange requires you to keep. The result is roughly how far, in percentage terms, the price can move against you before liquidation. Higher leverage shrinks that first term directly, which shrinks your entire allowed margin for error.

Here's the one sentence this formula actually proves, worth holding onto more than any specific number in this lesson. Leverage doesn't just magnify your gains, the part everyone already expects. It shrinks how wrong you're allowed to be, mechanically, by the exact same multiple, whether you're thinking about that trade-off or not.
Worked example.

Here's the five-times long, step by step, starting from an E.T.H. entry of three thousand dollars, at zero point five percent maintenance margin. One divided by five is zero point two. Subtract zero point five percent maintenance margin: zero point one nine five, or nineteen point five percent. At three thousand dollars entry, that's a liquidation price of roughly two thousand four hundred fifteen dollars.

Now the twenty-times short, the exact same entry price, and watch how dramatically less room remains. The five-times long survives roughly a nineteen-point-five-percent drop. The twenty-times short is liquidated by a price rise of only about four point five percent, a move E.T.H. can genuinely make within a single hour.

Worth being precise about what that four point five percent actually represents, in real market terms, not just as an abstract number. E.T.H., and most volatile crypto assets, can genuinely move that much within a single hour, during ordinary volatility, without any unusual news or event at all. Twenty-times leverage isn't a bet on direction alone; it's a bet that nothing routine happens in the meantime.

Quick check. Roughly how far can a 10x long fall before liquidation, at a 0.5% maintenance margin? The answer: about nine point five percent. One divided by ten is ten percent, minus zero point five percent maintenance margin.
The full curve.

Here's that same formula, run across six different leverage multiples, all at the same zero point five percent maintenance margin, so you can see the actual shape of the curve, not just two points on it. At two times leverage, you can be wrong by roughly forty-nine and a half percent. At three times, thirty-two point eight percent.
By ten times, you're down to nine and a half percent. And by fifty times, just one and a half percent, a move that can happen inside a single candle.

Notice how the curve isn't a straight line down; it falls fastest exactly where most people first add leverage, between two times and ten times. Going from two times to five times costs you thirty percentage points of room. Going from twenty times to fifty times only costs another three. The most dangerous leverage decision is usually the early one, not the extreme one.

Put another way. Doubling your leverage from two times to four times roughly halves your room to be wrong. Doubling it again, from four times to eight times, roughly halves it again. It's not a gentle slope; it's a halving, every time you double down.
Before you open the position.

Here's how you actually check your own liquidation price before opening anything, using this program's own calculator instead of guessing. You run defi_calc.py perp, passing your entry price, your chosen leverage, and your maintenance margin rate. It returns your exact liquidation price and the percentage move it represents.
Compare that percentage against how far the asset has actually moved on an ordinary day, not just on a good one, before you decide the leverage is reasonable.

Funding also matters more the longer you hold, so weigh it against your actual timeframe, not just the entry decision. A short hedge held for a few hours pays or receives only a few small funding settlements, a minor cost either way. The same position held open for months compounds every single settlement, and can quietly erode a position that looked fine on day one.

Here's your full checklist. Do it now, before opening any perp position. Isolated margin, by default, every time, not cross margin. Liquidation price computed and known, before you open, not after. Leverage kept at two to three times, or less, for anything except a hedge you fully understand. And funding cost checked specifically for however long you actually plan to hold.

Let's recap. A perp tracks price with no expiry; you post margin and choose leverage. Isolated margin risks only that position; cross margin risks your whole account. Mark price triggers liquidation specifically, smoothed against manipulation; funding keeps the perp tracking spot over time.
And the liquidation formula proves the real lesson: leverage shrinks your room to be wrong, by the same multiple it magnifies your gains, whether you're accounting for that or not.

Default to isolated margin, compute your liquidation price before opening, and keep leverage low unless you fully understand the hedge. Next up, Lesson three point six: a deep dive into lending design, e-mode, caps, auctions, and bad debt.
